rationale: I'm replacing the raw Pearson Fisher-z features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlation matrices on CC200 (no GSR). The reference point is the Riemannian mean of the training fold only. Abraham 2017 found this was the strongest classic pipeline on ABIDE, because it respects the curved geometry of correlation matrices and centres each subject on the group mean. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm replacing the single CC200 model with an equal-weight ensemble of the same tangent-space and logistic regression pipeline run on four parcellations: CC200, Harvard-Oxford, AAL and Dosenbach160. Each atlas carves the brain up differently, so their connectivity errors should be partly independent, and Abraham 2017 reported that atlas choice changes ABIDE results a lot. Averaging their decision scores should therefore give a more stable signal than any one atlas.

Inter-site differences are the biggest nuisance in ABIDE. Right now every subject is projected around one global geometric mean, so each site's scanner and protocol offset gets mixed into the connectivity features. This change re-centres each site separately (Riemannian Procrustes, as in Zanini 2018 and Ng 2014). Each subject's correlation matrix is whitened by its own site's Riemannian mean, computed label-free from that site's training and test matrices, before mapping to the tangent space at the identity. Site offsets should then disappear while the within-site connectivity differences linked to autism are kept.

The penalty strength C=0.001 was guessed, not tuned. With about 20k standardised tangent features and about 800 subjects, results in this p >> n setting depend heavily on regularisation. This change picks C from a log grid by AUROC in a grouped inner CV that uses only the training fold, with `ctx["groups_train"]` as the groups. The feature pipeline is unchanged.

CC200 may be too coarse to resolve the small, distributed connectivity differences linked to autism. Abraham 2017 found that finer parcellations of around 400 regions usually gave better tangent-space results on ABIDE. This change switches the same Ledoit-Wolf, tangent-space and L2 logistic regression pipeline from CC200 to CC400, the finer parcellation from the same family (~392 ROIs). That tests whether finer spatial resolution adds useful connectivity information, and nothing else changes. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a second view of the same CC200 data. Alongside the current no-GSR pipeline, the same Ledoit-Wolf, tangent-space and logistic regression model is fitted on the global-signal-regressed (`filt_global`) time series. The final score is the average of the two models' decision scores. GSR removes widespread motion and breathing signal but introduces anti-correlations, so the two versions should make partly independent errors on the same strong parcellation. That avoids the problem in round 2, where weaker atlases diluted the CC200 signal. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Each ROI's time series is z-scored before the correlation is computed, so the current model never sees how much each region fluctuates. In this band-passed data, that amplitude is an ALFF proxy, and altered ALFF has been reported in autism. This change adds a small second model: logistic regression on each ROI's log amplitude, centred within each subject to remove global scanner scaling. Its standardized decision score is averaged with the tangent-space model's score at half weight, so it adds information without replacing the strong connectivity signal. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

This adds a stacking step on top of the CC200 tangent-space model. A small second logistic regression combines the first model's out-of-fold decision score with age, sex and log mean framewise displacement (head motion). At C=0.001 among ~20k connectivity features, these covariates would get almost no weight if simply appended. Mean FD is a known confound (autistic participants tend to move more), so any gain partly reflects non-neural signal; I'm noting that openly rather than hiding it.

When I re-centred each site separately in round 3, the score dropped sharply. That suggests the dev pool's autism/control ratio differs by site, and since grouped CV puts the same sites in both training and test folds, the stage‑1 score can't pick that up by itself. This change adds one-hot site indicators (a legitimate covariate) to the second-stage logistic model alongside age, sex and log mean FD, so it can learn each site's baseline rate and calibration offset. This gain would be site base rates rather than brain signal, like the motion caveat in round 8. I haven't run it, so I have no Dev score yet.

Rounds 2 and 6 averaged other views with fixed equal weights, and weaker atlases diluted the strong CC200 signal. This change gives the second-stage logistic model each view's out-of-fold score as a separate input: CC200 without GSR, CC200 with GSR and Harvard-Oxford without GSR. The stacker can then learn how much each view adds alongside the covariates and site indicators, and down-weight a view that only adds noise. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Head motion and age both leave strong, label-independent marks on functional connectivity; motion in particular inflates short-range correlations. This change fits a linear regression on the training fold to remove age, log-age, sex and log mean FD from every tangent-space feature before the stage-1 logistic model, so that model can focus on neural signal. The second-stage model still receives these covariates directly, so any real predictive value they carry is kept.

Short, site-dependent scans make each subject's connectivity matrix a noisy estimate. This change trains stage 1 on the full-scan matrix plus two overlapping two-thirds-length crops per subject, all carrying the same label, and averages the three decision scores at test time. Crop augmentation like this was used in ASD-DiagNet / Dvornek on ABIDE, and the extra copies should make the classifier robust to estimation noise rather than fitting it. Inner CV keeps all crops of a subject together, and the stacker is unchanged. I haven't run this version, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

Round 3 re-centred every site and the score fell. The likely cause is that this also removed the site base-rate signal, and round 9 now gives that signal to the stacker through site one-hots. So I'm adding a second stage-1 view, a logistic model on tangent vectors with each site's mean subtracted (a ComBat-style location fix, label-free, using that site's train and test subjects), and feeding its out-of-fold score to stage 2 next to the original score. The stacker can then combine within-site connectivity differences with the site and covariate baselines. I have not run this version, so there is no Dev score yet.

Some sites have different autism/control ratios, so the stage-1 tangent-space logistic model can partly learn "which site" instead of autism-related connectivity, even though the stacker now handles site base rates through site one-hots. This change reweights stage-1 training samples so autism and controls carry equal total weight within each site. That removes the site–label link from stage-1 training without changing the features, which matters because removing site effects from the features themselves hurt in rounds 3 and 13.

Stage 1 currently treats every subject's connectivity matrix as equally reliable, even though high-motion scans (large mean FD) give corrupted, noisy correlation estimates. This change down-weights those scans when training the stage-1 model, with w_q = 1/(1+(FD/0.2)²). Within each site, autism and control still carry equal total weight after the quality weighting. The tangent-space classifier should then learn from cleaner connectivity patterns, while the stacker still receives mean FD directly. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

At the moment the stacker learns its weights on out-of-fold stage-1 scores from models trained on 80% of the training fold, but at test time it gets scores from a model trained on 100%. Those test scores are spread wider, so the connectivity score gets more weight relative to the site and covariate terms than the stacker intended. This change replaces the test-time score with the average of the five inner-fold models' predictions (cross-fit bagging), so training and test scores come from the same kind of model and should be on the same scale; averaging the five models should also make the test score less noisy.

The connectivity score is probably less reliable for some subjects than others. High-motion scans give noisier correlation estimates, and autism-related connectivity differences reportedly change with age (more connectivity in children, less in adults). So I'm adding score×age and score×log-mean-FD interaction terms to the second-stage logistic model. That lets the model trust the connectivity score more or less depending on a subject's age and motion. Stage 1 is unchanged, and I haven't run this version, so there's no Dev score yet.

I'm changing how ROIs outside the field of view (all-zero ROIs) are handled. Right now their correlation-matrix diagonal comes out at the small Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage value rather than 1, and their off-diagonals at 0, which the tangent-space log map turns into large outlier features that track field of view, and so site and scanner, rather than autism. Instead, I estimate the shrunk correlation only over each subject's valid ROIs and fill the missing rows and columns with the label-free cohort-mean correlation. Missing ROIs then sit near the reference point and carry roughly zero tangent-space signal.

Stage 1 currently z-scores each tangent-space feature on its own. That throws away the shared Riemannian metric of the tangent space and boosts low-variance edges, such as those involving noisy or partly out-of-view ROIs, to the same scale as the informative ones. This change centres the features and divides them all by one global RMS standard deviation instead. That keeps the overall strength of the C=0.001 penalty comparable, but the L2 penalty now treats every direction equally in the tangent space's own geometry, which should favour edges whose differences between subjects are actually large. I have not run this version, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

Ledoit-Wolf picks a separate shrinkage strength for each subject, and that strength depends mostly on scan length, which differs by site. This change estimates each subject's Ledoit-Wolf intensity, takes the median across the whole cohort without using labels, and applies that single shrinkage to every subject's correlation matrix. Correlations are then pulled toward identity by the same amount everywhere, which should remove a site-correlated nuisance from the tangent features while keeping the matrices well-conditioned. This is untested, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.
